History:
- Presenting complaint: several months of progressive anxiety, worst in the mornings with dread about leaving the house and work-related worry.
- Onset/duration: symptoms began approximately 2 months ago, coinciding with starting a new job.
- Triggers/context: new job in retail head office, difficult boss, worry about performance, public transport (tube) is stressful.
- Symptoms and course:
  - Morning-predominant anxiety with palpitations described as irregular; episodes last minutes up to ~10 minutes.
  - Insomnia: lying awake for hours, estimated total sleep ~3–4 hours/night, shallow sleep, waking with heart racing before alarm.
  - Daytime low energy, anhedonia, increased irritability/on edge.
  - Avoidance of social activities and hobbies (running, tennis); considering calling in sick but continues to attend work.
  - Appetite stable overall; increased consumption of chocolate.
  - Alcohol: reports drinking “quite a lot” on Friday/Saturday, occasional drinking during the week (exact amounts not provided).
  - Smoking: occasional smoker.
  - No history of prior similar episodes.
  - Denies suicidal ideation or intent.
  - Support: lives with parents; reports good family support; mother has history of depression.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic medical conditions documented in the transcript.
- Mental health history: no prior therapy; no prior diagnosed anxiety/depression documented.
- Medications: not documented.
- Allergies: not documented.
- Hospitalizations: not documented.

Physical Examination:
- No formal physical examination or vital signs recorded in the transcript.
- Reported/observed findings:
  - Patient alert and oriented (interaction intact).
  - Palpitations described as irregular; associated with anxiety and occasional chest discomfort when heart racing.
  - No objective chest pain reported outside palpitations.
  - No suicidal ideation.
- Relevant negatives:
  - Has not missed work due to symptoms.
  - No prior panic attacks reported.

Impression:
- Work-related anxiety with insomnia, palpitations, low mood and functional impact; palpitations most likely anxiety-associated (per clinician).

Management Plan:
- Offer/self-referral to NHS talking therapy (IAPT); clinician to send referral link.
- Provide online resources and written advice for sleep hygiene (clinician to add information to notes).
- Arrange basic blood tests to exclude medical triggers for palpitations (patient instructed to call support line to arrange tests).
- Arrange GP follow-up approximately one week after blood tests to review results.
- Medication for anxiety not recommended as first-line at this time; may be considered later if not improving.
- Safety netting: advised to contact GP if symptoms worsen or if unable to cope with work/activities.

Patient Summary:
- Patient developed progressive work-related anxiety over ~2 months after starting a new job, with morning palpitations, poor sleep, low mood, and reduced enjoyment of activities. Clinician advised talking therapy, provided self-help resources and sleep advice, recommended basic blood tests to investigate palpitations, and arranged GP follow-up one week after tests.

Key Takeaways:
- Self-refer to NHS talking therapy (IAPT) — clinician will send the link.
- Arrange recommended blood tests via the support line to exclude medical causes of palpitations.
- Contact GP urgently if symptoms worsen or if unable to cope with daily activities or work.

Next Steps:
- Patient to call support line to book basic blood tests.
- Clinician to send link for talking therapy and add sleep advice to medical notes.
- Schedule GP follow-up about 1 week after blood tests to review results and reassess need for further treatment (including medication if indicated).

Quality checks:
- Missing but expected elements: current medications, allergy list, past medical history details, vital signs, quantification of alcohol intake, smoking frequency, objective physical exam findings.
- Internal conflicts noted: when asked about chest pain the patient initially said “No” then later stated the fast heartbeat is painful—conflict regarding presence/severity of chest pain.
- Transcript quality: mostly clear and audible; occasional filler words and minor disfluencies but clinically relevant content intelligible.
